collins.hedgehog: None. Collins's comparison company never found a unifying concept. It grew by opportunistic acquisitions in drugstores and unrelated fields (department stores, security, food supply, later video rental) and depended on its founder.
hedgehog_key_points: should have committed to being the best drugstore operator in its region
collins.stop_doing: Stop unrelated diversification (department stores, security services, food-service supply, and later video stores) and concentrate on drugstores.
stop_doing_key_points: exit or stop buying non-drugstore businesses
stop growth-by-acquisition without a unifying concept
collins.leader_type: Not Level 5. Collins portrays founder Jack Eckerd as a talented, dominant individual (a 'genius with a thousand helpers' pattern) whose attention went to politics; when he stepped away the company had no strong team or concept to carry on.
brutal_facts: the founder is absorbed by politics
diversified businesses dilute focus and capital
the largest national chain has entered its home state

later_history: Jack Eckerd left to head the U.S. General Services Administration in 1975; Stewart Turley became chairman. The 1977 purchase of the North Carolina Eckerd chain made it the second-largest U.S. drug chain (766 stores); sales passed $1B by 1978. Bought a video-store chain in 1980 and sold it, with the department stores, in 1985. Taken private in a Merrill Lynch-led leveraged buyout in 1986; public again in 1993. Bought by J.C. Penney in 1997 ($3.3B), which later closed hundreds of stores and took a $1.3B charge on its sale. Split in 2004 between CVS and Jean Coutu; Rite Aid bought the Jean Coutu stores in 2007 and retired the Eckerd name.
notes: Direct comparison company for A19 (Walgreens). Collins's 'genius with a thousand helpers' characterization of Eckerd is from memory of Ch. 2 and was not verified online; the phrase is quoted as a short label only.
